description:
Programadora de Bordo – Helena Duarte

Helena Duarte é daquelas alunas que lideram com organização, determinação e criatividade. Aluna da 1ª série do Ensino Médio, é apaixonada por música, astronomia e curiosidades científicas. Vive com fones no ouvido, mas adora explicar fenômenos do universo. Essa mistura de lógica e criatividade a levou à programação, que vê como uma música: exige ritmo, estrutura e imaginação. Na equipe, será a ponte entre a ideia e a execução.
summary:
Our application’s primary goal is to spark interest in space exploration among children and teenagers, encouraging them to dream of becoming astronauts and to understand the real-world challenges of living beyond Earth.

Through an interactive and educational experience, users can manage an outpost on the Moon or Mars, making critical decisions to ensure the survival of a team of astronauts. Throughout the simulation, they must balance limited resources—such as energy, oxygen, water, and food production—while navigating challenges like exposure to space radiation, facility protection, communications, and the development of scientific research.

Every choice carries consequences and costs that accumulate over time, allowing participants to grasp how strategic decisions can determine the success or failure of a space mission.

The concept is to transform scientific ideas—such as lunar radiation, extraterrestrial environmental conditions, and survival technologies—into knowledge that is both accessible and engaging for a young audience. Unlike traditional educational materials, which often present information in an abstract or overly technical way, our application offers a hands-on, playful, and immersive learning experience, bringing students closer to science, technology, and future space exploration missions.
details:
LunaBase is an interactive educational application designed to spark interest among children and adolescents—aged 8 to 18—in space exploration and the future possibilities for human habitation beyond Earth.

LunaBase offers a simulation experience in which students take on the responsibility of managing a human base on the Moon or Mars. Their challenge is to understand and address the issues that will determine the survival of a team of astronauts in extraterrestrial environments.

Throughout the experience, participants explore fundamental topics such as oxygen availability, air quality, water supply and recycling, space agriculture, energy production and storage, protection against solar radiation and cosmic rays, extreme temperatures, astronaut health, and communication with Earth.

The application also covers essential scientific concepts, including gravitational differences between Earth, the Moon, and Mars, the characteristics of the Martian atmosphere, extraterrestrial natural resources, and life-support technologies. Students can learn about real-world space missions—such as Apollo and Artemis—gaining insight into the evolution of human exploration and the challenges facing future crewed missions to Mars.

Through missions, challenges, levels, scoring, rankings, and achievements, LunaBase transforms scientific content into an engaging learning journey. A key feature is that it places the student in charge of an entire team’s survival, fostering strategic thinking and an understanding of the scientific, technological, and ethical decisions involved in space exploration.

The project integrates knowledge from mathematics, physics, chemistry, biology, engineering, and technology, demonstrating that the conquest of new worlds relies on collaboration across various fields of study.

Developed with the support of the Manus AI platform, LunaBase is currently in the stage of a navigable prototype, with plans to expand its features.

Our greatest ambition goes beyond teaching how to survive on the Moon or Mars: we aim to inspire future careers. We want a child who never imagined working in science to discover, through this experience, that they too can become an astronaut, scientist, engineer, or researcher.

Because humanity’s future in space begins with imagination, but it will be built by the knowledge of the generations to come.
dataRefs: NASA's central public API portal, providing free programmatic access to datasets including the Astronomy Picture of the Day (APOD), Mars Rover Photos, and the Space Weather Database (DONKI). A free API key (higher rate limits than the shared demo key) can be requested instantly and is a good starting point for any challenge team building a data-connected prototype.

Real radiation dose measurements recorded by dosimetry instruments aboard the International Space Station, contributed by multiple international space agencies. Provides authentic astronaut radiation exposure data (e.g., absorbed dose rate) useful for any tool modeling shielding, health risk, or long-duration mission trade-offs.

An interactive visualization and data-download portal for real Mars surface imagery, elevation, and terrain data compiled from NASA's Mars missions (including Curiosity and Perseverance). Useful for teams wanting real environmental or geographic data to ground a Mars outpost site or terrain visualization in actual surface conditions.
projectRefs: The CSA's Space Resources for STEM and Youth Organizations page provides free, bilingual tools and activities to help educators engage youth in space and STEM. Designed for museums, libraries, camps, after-school clubs, community groups, and outreach organizations, these resources support learning beyond the classroom.

This web package is a one-stop resource for educators and youth who want to learn about food in space. This toolkit aims to outline how food production in space can relate to the health and nutrition of astronauts as well as benefit humans on Earth.
